chapters.title: Kubernetes Basics
chapters.summary: Pods, Deployments, Services, Ingress, ConfigMaps, Secrets, probes and resources: enough Kubernetes to deploy and debug a web app.

lesson.heading: What Kubernetes does
lesson.body:
Kubernetes (K8s) is a container orchestrator. You declare the **desired state** ("run 3 replicas of image app:abc123, expose them on port 80") and **controllers** continuously reconcile the actual state toward it: restarting crashed containers, rescheduling pods from failed nodes, and rolling out new versions.

Architecture in brief:

- **Control plane**: the API server (everything talks to it), etcd (the state store), the scheduler (assigns pods to nodes) and controller managers. Managed services (EKS, GKE, AKS) run this for you.
- **Nodes**: worker machines running the kubelet (starts containers via a runtime such as containerd) and kube-proxy (service networking).

You interact with `kubectl` and YAML manifests, usually applied by CI or a GitOps tool such as Argo CD or Flux.

lesson.heading: Pods and Deployments
lesson.body:
A **Pod** is the smallest deployable unit: one or more containers that share a network namespace (same IP, talk over localhost) and can share volumes. Pods are ephemeral and get new IPs when recreated, so you rarely create them directly.

A **Deployment** manages a **ReplicaSet**, which keeps N identical pods running. Changing the pod template (for example the image tag) triggers a rolling update; `kubectl rollout undo deployment/api` rolls back.

Other workload types: **StatefulSet** (stable identities and per-pod storage, for databases), **DaemonSet** (one pod per node, for log agents), **Job/CronJob** (run to completion, scheduled tasks).

code.source:
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels: { app: api }
  template:
    metadata:
      labels: { app: api }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: api
          image: ghcr.io/acme/api:3f9c2e1
          ports:
            - containerPort: 3000
          envFrom:
            - configMapRef: { name: api-config }
            - secretRef: { name: api-secrets }
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: 250m, memory: 256Mi }
            limits: { memory: 512Mi }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz/ready, port: 3000 }
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /healthz/live, port: 3000 }
            initialDelaySeconds: 10

lesson.heading: Services and Ingress
lesson.body:
A **Service** gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name (`api.default.svc.cluster.local`, or just `api` within the namespace) in front of a changing set of pods selected by **labels**.

- `ClusterIP` (default): reachable only inside the cluster.
- `NodePort`: opens a port on every node.
- `LoadBalancer`: provisions a cloud load balancer.
- Headless (`clusterIP: None`): DNS returns pod IPs directly, used with StatefulSets.

An **Ingress** defines HTTP routing (host and path based) from outside to Services, implemented by an **ingress controller** (ingress-nginx, Traefik, AWS Load Balancer Controller). Without a controller installed, Ingress objects do nothing. The newer **Gateway API** (Gateway, HTTPRoute) is the successor with richer, role-oriented routing and is the direction new setups are moving.

code.source:
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: api
spec:
  selector: { app: api }
  ports:
    - port: 80
      targetPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: web
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
    - hosts: [app.example.com]
      secretName: app-tls
  rules:
    - host: app.example.com
      http:
        paths:
          - path: /api
            pathType: Prefix
            backend:
              service: { name: api, port: { number: 80 } }

lesson.heading: ConfigMaps, Secrets, probes and resources
lesson.body:
**ConfigMaps** hold non-sensitive config; **Secrets** hold sensitive values. Both can be exposed as env vars or mounted files. Important: Secrets are only **base64 encoded**, not encrypted, by default. Enable encryption at rest for etcd, restrict access with RBAC, and consider External Secrets Operator or a CSI driver to sync from AWS Secrets Manager or Vault. Env vars from ConfigMaps do not update in running pods; restart the Deployment (`kubectl rollout restart`).

**Probes**:

- **Readiness**: is the pod ready to receive traffic? Failing removes it from Service endpoints but does not restart it.
- **Liveness**: is the process stuck? Failing restarts the container. Do not check dependencies (like the DB) in liveness, or a DB blip restarts every pod.
- **Startup**: holds off the other probes for slow-starting apps.

**Resources**: `requests` are what the scheduler reserves; `limits` are hard caps. Exceeding the memory limit gets the container **OOMKilled**; exceeding CPU limits causes throttling. A common practice is setting memory request equal to the limit and avoiding tight CPU limits. A **HorizontalPodAutoscaler** scales replicas based on CPU utilization relative to requests or on custom metrics.

lesson.heading: Debugging with kubectl
lesson.body:
The commands that solve most problems:

- `kubectl get pods -o wide`: status, restarts, node.
- `kubectl describe pod <name>`: events at the bottom explain scheduling failures, image pull errors, probe failures, OOMKilled.
- `kubectl logs <pod> [-c container] [--previous]`: `--previous` shows logs of the crashed instance.
- `kubectl exec -it <pod> -- sh`: shell into a container.
- `kubectl port-forward svc/api 8080:80`: reach a ClusterIP service locally.
- `kubectl get endpoints api` (or EndpointSlices): empty means the Service selector matches no ready pods.
- `kubectl rollout status|history|undo deployment/api`.

Common statuses: **ImagePullBackOff** (wrong image name/tag or missing registry credentials), **CrashLoopBackOff** (container keeps exiting: check `logs --previous`), **Pending** (no node has enough requested CPU/memory, or an unbound volume), **OOMKilled** (raise memory limit or fix the leak).

keyPoints: Kubernetes reconciles declared desired state; controllers fix drift continuously.
Pods are ephemeral; Deployments manage ReplicaSets and rolling updates with rollback.
Services select pods by label and provide stable DNS; Ingress (via a controller) routes external HTTP.
Secrets are base64, not encrypted, by default: enable encryption at rest and RBAC.
Readiness gates traffic, liveness restarts containers; keep dependencies out of liveness checks.
Requests drive scheduling; exceeding the memory limit causes OOMKilled.
`kubectl describe` events and `logs --previous` diagnose most failures.

questions.prompt: Which object provides a stable DNS name and virtual IP for a set of pods?
questions.explanation: A Service selects pods by label and load balances across them behind a stable name, even as pod IPs change.

questions.prompt: A pod shows status CrashLoopBackOff. What is the best first command?
questions.explanation: CrashLoopBackOff means the container keeps exiting. `--previous` shows the logs of the last crashed instance, which usually contain the error.

questions.prompt: A pod's readiness probe starts failing. What happens?
options: The pod is removed from Service endpoints and stops receiving traffic, but is not restarted
questions.explanation: Readiness controls traffic routing. Liveness failures are what trigger restarts.

questions.prompt: Your Ingress resource is created but nothing routes traffic. What is the most likely reason?
options: No ingress controller is installed (or the ingressClassName does not match one)
Services cannot be used with Ingress
questions.explanation: Ingress is only a configuration object. An ingress controller (ingress-nginx, Traefik, ALB controller) must watch and implement it.

questions.prompt: Which workload type fits a Postgres cluster where each replica needs a stable name and its own persistent volume?
questions.explanation: StatefulSets give pods stable ordinal identities (db-0, db-1) and volumeClaimTemplates for per-pod storage.

questions.prompt: A container repeatedly shows `OOMKilled`. What does that mean?
options: It exceeded its memory limit and the kernel killed it
The image could not be pulled
questions.explanation: Memory is not compressible: exceeding the memory limit kills the process. CPU over-limit only causes throttling.

questions.prompt: Kubernetes Secrets are encrypted by default because their values are base64 encoded.
questions.explanation: Base64 is an encoding, trivially reversible. Encryption at rest must be configured (managed clusters often offer KMS envelope encryption), and access restricted via RBAC.

questions.prompt: Containers in the same pod can reach each other on localhost.
questions.explanation: Containers in a pod share one network namespace, so they share an IP and port space. This enables sidecar patterns.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which can cause a pod to stay in Pending?
options: No node has enough unreserved CPU/memory for its requests
A PersistentVolumeClaim it uses is not bound
Its application throws an exception at startup
Node taints it does not tolerate / unsatisfiable node affinity
questions.explanation: Pending means not yet scheduled or started. App exceptions cause CrashLoopBackOff, and readiness failures leave the pod Running but not Ready.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: To roll a Deployment back to its previous revision, run `kubectl rollout ___ deployment/api`.
questions.explanation: `kubectl rollout undo` reverts to the previous ReplicaSet revision; `--to-revision` targets a specific one.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between liveness, readiness and startup probes, and a common mistake with each.
questions.answer:
- Readiness: decides if the pod receives traffic. Mistake: none configured, so traffic hits pods before they warm up, or during shutdown. It can check critical dependencies carefully.
- Liveness: decides if the container must be restarted because it is wedged. Mistake: checking the database or other dependencies, so a dependency outage restarts every pod and makes things worse; or too aggressive timeouts that kill a busy but healthy app.
- Startup: protects slow-starting apps by disabling liveness/readiness until it succeeds. Mistake: using a long liveness initialDelaySeconds instead, which delays detection of real hangs forever after.
- Also: handle SIGTERM and fail readiness during shutdown so the pod is removed from endpoints before exiting.

questions.prompt: A Service returns connection refused / no endpoints. How do you debug it?
questions.answer:
- `kubectl get endpoints <svc>` or `kubectl get endpointslices -l kubernetes.io/service-name=<svc>`: if empty, the Service selector does not match any ready pods.
- Compare `kubectl get svc <svc> -o yaml` selector with pod labels (`kubectl get pods --show-labels`). Typos are common.
- If pods match but are not Ready, check readiness probe failures in `kubectl describe pod`.
- Check `targetPort` matches the container's listening port and the app binds to 0.0.0.0, not 127.0.0.1.
- Test from inside the cluster: `kubectl run tmp --rm -it --image=busybox -- wget -qO- http://svc:port`.
- Check NetworkPolicies that might block traffic, and namespace (DNS `svc.namespace`).

questions.prompt: How do requests, limits and the HorizontalPodAutoscaler work together?
questions.answer:
- Requests are the guaranteed reservation used by the scheduler to place pods; the sum of requests on a node cannot exceed its allocatable capacity.
- Limits cap usage: memory over limit -> OOMKilled; CPU over limit -> throttled. Pods with requests = limits for all resources get Guaranteed QoS and are evicted last.
- HPA computes desired replicas from observed metrics vs targets, for example average CPU utilization as a percentage of requests: if pods use 90% of requests and the target is 60%, it scales up by about 1.5x.
- So bad requests break autoscaling: too low and HPA scales too eagerly and nodes overcommit; too high and you waste capacity.
- Cluster Autoscaler or Karpenter then adds nodes when pods are Pending for lack of capacity.

chapters.title: Infrastructure as Code with Terraform
chapters.summary: Declarative infrastructure with Terraform: providers, resources, state, modules, plans in CI and handling drift safely.

lesson.heading: Why Infrastructure as Code
lesson.body:
Clicking resources together in a cloud console is unrepeatable, unreviewable and undocumented. **Infrastructure as Code (IaC)** defines infrastructure in versioned files, so changes go through pull requests, environments are reproducible, and disaster recovery is re-applying code.

Tools:

- **Terraform** (HashiCorp, BSL license) and **OpenTofu** (the open-source MPL fork under the Linux Foundation, largely compatible): declarative HCL, multi-cloud via providers.
- **AWS CloudFormation / CDK**: AWS-native; CDK lets you write TypeScript that synthesizes CloudFormation.
- **Pulumi**: real programming languages (TypeScript, Python, Go) with its own engine.

Declarative means you describe the end state; the tool computes the diff from current state and applies only what is needed.

lesson.heading: Core workflow: init, plan, apply
lesson.body:
- `terraform init`: downloads providers and modules, configures the backend.
- `terraform fmt` and `terraform validate`: formatting and static validation.
- `terraform plan`: shows what will be created (+), changed (~), destroyed (-) or replaced (-/+). Always read it; a `-/+` on a database means data loss.
- `terraform apply`: executes the plan. In CI, save the plan with `-out=tfplan` and apply exactly that file.
- `terraform destroy`: tears everything down.

Resources reference each other (`aws_s3_bucket.uploads.id`), which builds a dependency graph; Terraform creates independent resources in parallel and dependent ones in order.

lesson.heading: State: the most important concept
lesson.body:
Terraform keeps a **state file** mapping resources in code to real cloud objects (IDs, attributes). Without it, Terraform cannot know what it manages.

- Store state **remotely** (S3, HCP Terraform, GCS, Azure Blob), never only on a laptop, and never commit it to Git: it can contain secrets in plain text, such as generated database passwords.
- Use **state locking** so two applies cannot run at once and corrupt state. Historically on AWS this was a DynamoDB table; newer Terraform versions support S3 native locking via `use_lockfile = true`.
- Enable bucket versioning and encryption for the state bucket.
- Split state by environment and component (network, data, app) to limit blast radius and speed up plans.

State operations: `terraform import` (or `import` blocks) to adopt existing resources, `terraform state mv` (or `moved` blocks) when refactoring names, `terraform state rm` to stop managing something without deleting it.

lesson.heading: Variables, modules and environments
lesson.body:
**Input variables** parameterize config; **outputs** expose values; **locals** hold computed values. Mark sensitive values with `sensitive = true` to hide them in plan output (they are still in state).

**Modules** are reusable packages of resources (a folder with inputs and outputs). Use them for patterns repeated across environments, like 'a VPC' or 'an ECS service with ALB'. Pin module versions. The public Terraform Registry has well-maintained community modules (for example `terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws`).

Environments: the common approaches are a directory per environment (`envs/staging`, `envs/prod`) that each call shared modules with different variables, or workspaces. Separate directories with separate state and separate cloud accounts give the strongest isolation.

`count` and `for_each` create multiple instances. Prefer `for_each` with a map: with `count`, removing an item from the middle of a list shifts indexes and forces unnecessary destroy/recreate.

lesson.heading: Terraform in CI, drift and safety
lesson.body:
A mature workflow:

- On PR: `fmt -check`, `validate`, lint (tflint), security scan (Checkov, Trivy), then `plan` and post the plan as a PR comment.
- On merge: apply the reviewed plan with credentials from OIDC, with an environment approval for production.
- Tools such as Atlantis, HCP Terraform, Spacelift or env0 automate this.

**Drift** is when real infrastructure differs from code because someone changed it manually. `terraform plan` shows the drift; you either codify the change or let apply revert it. Run scheduled plans to detect drift and restrict console write access.

Safety features:

- `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` on databases and state buckets.
- `create_before_destroy` for zero-downtime replacement.
- `ignore_changes` for attributes managed elsewhere (for example a desired count changed by autoscaling).
- Read `-/+ must be replaced` lines carefully: changing some attributes (like an RDS identifier) forces replacement.

keyPoints: IaC makes infrastructure reviewable, reproducible and recoverable through version control.
init -> plan -> apply; in CI, apply the saved plan that was reviewed.
State maps code to real resources: store it remotely, encrypted, versioned and locked; never in Git.
Sensitive values still land in state, so protect the state backend like a secret.
Use modules with pinned versions; prefer `for_each` over `count` for stable addressing.
Drift = manual changes; detect with scheduled plans and limit console access.
Guard critical resources with `prevent_destroy` and read replace (-/+) actions carefully.

questions.prompt: What does the Terraform state file primarily do?
options: Maps resources in configuration to real-world objects and their attributes
questions.explanation: State binds `aws_s3_bucket.uploads` to the actual bucket, enabling Terraform to compute diffs and track dependencies.

questions.prompt: Two engineers run `terraform apply` on the same state at the same time. What prevents corruption?
questions.explanation: Remote backends with locking (S3 lockfile, DynamoDB, HCP Terraform) ensure only one operation modifies state at a time.

questions.prompt: A plan shows `-/+ resource "aws_db_instance" "main" (must be replaced)`. What should you do?
options: Stop and investigate: replacing a database destroys it and its data unless handled
questions.explanation: A forced replacement of a stateful resource means destroy and recreate. Find the attribute causing it, and protect such resources with prevent_destroy.

questions.prompt: Given `count = length(var.names)` with names ["a", "b", "c"], you remove "a". What happens?
options: Indexes shift, so b and c are seen as changed/replaced and the last index is destroyed
questions.explanation: count addresses by index: [0]=a,[1]=b,[2]=c becomes [0]=b,[1]=c. Terraform updates or replaces [0] and [1] and destroys [2]. `for_each` with keys avoids this.

questions.prompt: Where should Terraform state for a team project be stored?
options: In a remote backend with encryption, versioning and locking
In a public S3 bucket for easy access
questions.explanation: State can contain secrets and must be shared safely. Remote encrypted, versioned, locked storage is the standard.

questions.prompt: Someone changed a security group manually in the AWS console. What is this called and how do you see it?
questions.explanation: Plan refreshes real state and shows differences from configuration. Apply will revert the manual change unless you codify it.

questions.prompt: Marking a variable `sensitive = true` keeps its value out of the state file.
questions.explanation: It only redacts the value in CLI output. The value is still stored in state in plain text, which is why state must be protected.

questions.prompt: OpenTofu is an open-source fork of Terraform that is largely compatible with Terraform configurations.
questions.explanation: OpenTofu forked after HashiCorp moved Terraform to the BSL license in 2023 and is maintained under the Linux Foundation.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which belong in a Terraform pull request pipeline?
options: terraform plan posted to the PR
questions.explanation: PR checks verify formatting, validity, security and show the plan for review. Destroy has no place in a PR pipeline.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: To stop Terraform from ever deleting a resource, set `lifecycle { ___ = true }`.
questions.explanation: prevent_destroy makes any plan that would destroy the resource fail with an error.

questions.prompt: How would you structure Terraform for a company with dev, staging and production on AWS?
questions.answer:
- Separate AWS accounts per environment (via AWS Organizations) for blast-radius and IAM isolation.
- Reusable internal modules (network, ecs-service, rds, monitoring) with versioned releases.
- Per-environment root configurations (`live/prod/network`, `live/prod/app`...) calling modules with env-specific variables, each with its own remote state and lock; split by component so a change to the app does not plan the whole VPC.
- Pass values between stacks via outputs and `terraform_remote_state` or SSM parameters.
- CI: fmt, validate, tflint, Checkov, plan on PR with plan comment; apply saved plan on merge via OIDC role per account, production gated by approval.
- Guardrails: prevent_destroy on data stores, scheduled drift detection, policy as code (OPA/Sentinel) for things like 'no public S3 buckets'.

questions.prompt: You need to bring a manually created RDS instance under Terraform management. How?
questions.answer:
- Write the matching `aws_db_instance` resource in code.
- Use an `import` block (`import { to = aws_db_instance.main  id = "mydb" }`) and run plan; newer Terraform can even generate config with `terraform plan -generate-config-out=generated.tf`. The older CLI `terraform import` also works.
- Iterate until plan shows no changes, meaning code matches reality; do not apply while it shows a replacement.
- Add `lifecycle { prevent_destroy = true }` and possibly `ignore_changes` for attributes changed by operations (like minor engine version with auto-upgrade).
- Move secrets (master password) to Secrets Manager / `manage_master_user_password` rather than plain variables.

questions.prompt: Compare Terraform with AWS CDK or Pulumi. When would you pick each?
questions.answer:
- Terraform/OpenTofu: declarative HCL, huge provider ecosystem (AWS, Cloudflare, Datadog, GitHub, Vercel), mature tooling for plans, policy and drift. Best for multi-cloud or multi-vendor infrastructure and platform teams.
- AWS CDK: TypeScript/Python constructs synthesizing CloudFormation; AWS-native with high-level constructs and CloudFormation's managed state and rollbacks. Good for AWS-only teams who want to stay in TypeScript, and app teams deploying serverless stacks.
- Pulumi: general-purpose languages over its own engine and multi-cloud providers; strong for teams wanting loops, abstractions and testing in real code.
- Trade-offs: real languages allow powerful abstractions but also complexity and non-determinism; HCL is constrained but readable to ops. Choose based on team skills, cloud footprint and existing ecosystem.

chapters.title: Observability: Logs, Metrics, Traces and SLOs
chapters.summary: Instrument services with structured logs, metrics and distributed traces using OpenTelemetry, and alert on SLOs instead of noise.

lesson.heading: Monitoring vs observability
lesson.body:
**Monitoring** answers known questions: is CPU high, is the site up, is the error rate above 1%? **Observability** is the ability to answer new questions about system behavior from the telemetry it emits, without shipping new code, such as "why are checkout requests from Android users in Germany slow since 14:00?"

The three main signals:

- **Logs**: timestamped events with context. Great detail, expensive at volume.
- **Metrics**: numeric aggregates over time (counters, gauges, histograms). Cheap to store and ideal for dashboards and alerts.
- **Traces**: the path of one request across services as a tree of **spans**, each with timing and attributes. Ideal for latency and dependency analysis.

Profiles (continuous profiling) are increasingly treated as a fourth signal. The power comes from correlating them: a metric spike links to example traces, and traces link to the logs of each span via a shared `trace_id`.

lesson.heading: Structured logging
lesson.body:
Log JSON, not free text, so log platforms can filter and aggregate by field. Include a timestamp, level, message, service name, environment, request or trace ID, and relevant business IDs (userId, orderId).

- Use a fast logger like **pino** in Node; write to stdout (12-factor) and let the platform ship logs (CloudWatch, Loki, Datadog, Elastic).
- Use levels deliberately: `error` for actionable failures, `warn` for degraded behavior, `info` for business events, `debug` off in production by default.
- **Never log secrets or sensitive personal data**: passwords, tokens, full card numbers. Use the logger's redaction feature.
- Log volume costs money; sample noisy success logs and rely on metrics for counts.

lesson.heading: Metrics: RED, USE and the four golden signals
lesson.body:
Metric types: **counter** (only goes up: requests_total), **gauge** (goes up and down: memory, queue depth), **histogram** (distribution of values in buckets: request duration), which lets you compute percentiles.

Useful frameworks:

- **RED** for services: Rate (requests/s), Errors (failed/s), Duration (latency distribution).
- **USE** for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors (CPU, disk, connection pools).
- Google SRE's **four golden signals**: latency, traffic, errors, saturation.

Watch percentiles, not averages: p50 can look fine while p99 users wait 8 seconds. Also beware **high cardinality** labels: adding `userId` or a full URL as a metric label creates millions of time series and can take down Prometheus or explode your bill. Put high-cardinality data in traces and logs instead.

Prometheus scrapes metrics from a `/metrics` endpoint and is queried with PromQL; Grafana is the common dashboarding layer. Managed alternatives include CloudWatch, Datadog and Grafana Cloud.

lesson.heading: Distributed tracing with OpenTelemetry
lesson.body:
**OpenTelemetry (OTel)** is the CNCF standard for generating and exporting telemetry: vendor-neutral APIs and SDKs, auto-instrumentation libraries (HTTP, Express, pg, Redis, fetch), the **OTLP** protocol, and the **Collector** which receives, processes (batching, sampling, redaction) and exports to any backend (Jaeger, Tempo, Honeycomb, Datadog, X-Ray).

Trace context propagates between services through the W3C `traceparent` HTTP header, so a trace can follow a request from the browser through the API gateway, services, queues and the database.

**Sampling** controls cost: head sampling decides at the start (keep 10%), tail sampling (in the Collector) decides after the trace completes, so you can keep all errors and slow traces while dropping most healthy ones.

In Next.js, `instrumentation.ts` with `@vercel/otel` or the OTel Node SDK registers tracing at startup.

lesson.heading: SLIs, SLOs, error budgets and alerting
lesson.body:
An **SLI** (indicator) measures user experience, for example the proportion of requests served successfully in under 300 ms. An **SLO** (objective) is the target: 99.9% over 30 days. An **SLA** is a contractual promise with penalties, usually looser than the SLO.

The **error budget** is `1 - SLO`: 99.9% over 30 days allows about 43 minutes of badness. If the budget is healthy, ship faster; if it is burning, prioritize reliability work.

Alerting principles:

- Alert on **symptoms users feel** (SLO burn rate, error rate, latency), not on every cause (CPU at 80%).
- Use **multi-window burn-rate alerts**: page when the budget burns fast (for example 14x over 1 hour), ticket when it burns slowly.
- Every page must be actionable and link to a runbook; noisy alerts cause alert fatigue and missed incidents.
- After incidents, run **blameless postmortems** focused on systemic fixes.

keyPoints: Logs, metrics and traces answer different questions; correlate them through a shared trace ID.
Log structured JSON to stdout with context IDs, and redact secrets and personal data.
Use RED for services and USE for resources; watch p95/p99, not averages.
Avoid high-cardinality metric labels like user IDs; put that detail in traces and logs.
OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard: SDK + auto-instrumentation + OTLP + Collector.
Trace context propagates via the W3C `traceparent` header; tail sampling keeps errors and slow traces.
Define SLOs and error budgets; alert on burn rate and user-facing symptoms, with runbooks.

questions.prompt: Which signal is best for finding which downstream service made one specific request slow?
questions.explanation: A trace shows each span's timing across services, so you can see exactly which call consumed the latency.

questions.prompt: An engineer adds a `user_id` label to the `http_requests_total` Prometheus metric for a 5 million user app. What is the problem?
options: It creates millions of time series (high cardinality), exploding memory and cost
questions.explanation: Each unique label combination is a separate series. Unbounded labels like user IDs belong in traces or logs.

questions.prompt: Average latency is 120 ms but users complain about slowness. What should you look at?
options: Tail percentiles like p95 and p99
questions.explanation: Averages hide the tail. A small slow fraction can be invisible in the mean but painful for many users (and every user over many requests).

questions.prompt: An SLO is 99.9% availability over 30 days. Roughly how much full downtime does the error budget allow?
questions.explanation: 0.1% of 30 days = 0.001 x 43,200 minutes = 43.2 minutes.

questions.prompt: How is trace context passed from one service to another over HTTP in OpenTelemetry by default?
questions.explanation: OTel uses W3C Trace Context by default: `traceparent` carries trace ID, parent span ID and flags.

questions.prompt: Which alert is most aligned with SRE best practice?
options: Page when CPU > 70% on any node
Page when the checkout SLO error budget is burning at 14x the sustainable rate over the last hour
questions.explanation: Burn-rate alerts tie paging to user impact and urgency. Cause-based thresholds (CPU) are noisy and often not actionable.

questions.prompt: Tail sampling can keep 100% of error traces while discarding most successful ones.
questions.explanation: Tail sampling decides after the trace is complete (usually in the OTel Collector), so it can filter by status and latency.

questions.prompt: Logging full request bodies, including passwords and tokens, is fine as long as logs are stored privately.
questions.explanation: Logs are widely accessible, replicated and retained; secrets in logs are a common breach source and a compliance violation. Redact them.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which are components or features of OpenTelemetry?
questions.explanation: OTel generates, processes and exports telemetry. Storage and visualization come from backends like Jaeger, Tempo, Grafana or vendors.

questions.prompt: Fill the blank: The service-level metrics framework of Rate, Errors and Duration is abbreviated ___.
questions.explanation: RED (Tom Wilkie) covers request-driven services; USE (Brendan Gregg) covers resources.

questions.prompt: How would you add observability to an existing Node.js microservices system with none today?
questions.answer:
- Start with structured JSON logs (pino) to stdout with request IDs, shipped to a central store.
- Add OpenTelemetry SDK with auto-instrumentation in every service (HTTP, Express/Fastify, pg, Redis, fetch, messaging), exporting OTLP to an OTel Collector; the Collector batches, samples (tail sampling keeping errors and slow traces) and exports to the chosen backend.
- Inject trace_id into logs to correlate; propagate context through queues by putting `traceparent` in message headers.
- Emit RED metrics per endpoint (histograms) and USE metrics for pools and queues; build dashboards per service.
- Define SLOs for key user journeys (login, checkout) and set burn-rate alerts with runbooks.
- Roll out incrementally starting at the edge (gateway) and highest-traffic services, and control cost via sampling and label hygiene.

questions.prompt: p99 latency of an API doubled after a deploy, but p50 is unchanged. How do you investigate?
questions.answer:
- Confirm correlation with the deploy (deploy markers on dashboards) and consider rolling back first if the SLO is burning.
- Break down latency by endpoint, region, instance and version to see whether it is isolated (canary vs baseline).
- Pull exemplar traces from the slow tail: which span grew? Common culprits are a new N+1 query, a missing index, a synchronous external call, lock contention, or a connection pool exhausted under load.
- Check saturation metrics: DB pool wait time, event loop lag in Node (GC pauses or CPU-heavy work blocking the loop), CPU throttling from container limits.
- Compare profiles before/after if continuous profiling exists.
- Fix, add a regression test or performance check, and document in a postmortem.

questions.prompt: Explain SLI, SLO, SLA and error budgets, and how they change engineering decisions.
questions.answer:
- SLI: a measured ratio of good events to total, for example successful requests under 300 ms / all requests.
- SLO: the internal target for that SLI over a window, for example 99.9% per 28 days.
- SLA: an external contract with consequences, set looser than the SLO so you breach the SLO first.
- Error budget: 1 - SLO, the amount of unreliability you can spend.
- Decisions: when budget remains, teams ship features and take risks (faster deploys, experiments); when it is exhausted, a freeze or reliability focus kicks in. It turns the 'velocity vs stability' argument into data both product and engineering agreed to, and drives alerting via burn rates instead of arbitrary thresholds.
